title: Alexandra de Gendre
text:
I am the 2022 McKenzie Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Department of Economics at the University of Melbourne. Since 2026 I am also a CNRS Research Fellow affiliated with CREST in Paris.  
I am an economist interested in applied microeconomics, applied econometrics and the formation of human capital. I study how children’s health and education is shaped by their parents, teachers, peers, and education and welfare policies. I am also interested in meta-science and methods to improve the reliability of our empirical research findings. My McKenzie Fellowship project focuses on methods to synthesize and generalize empirical findings in the case of peer effects and teacher role model effects on student performance.




The Department of Economics at the University of Melbourne since February 2022

CNRS Research Fellow, CREST, Paris since February 2026

IZA Institute of Labor Economics since July 2018

Australian Research Council (ARC) Centre of Excellence for Children and Families over the Life Course (LCC) since May 2018





I completed my Ph.D. in Economics from Maastricht University in the Netherlands in 2021 under the supervision of Prof. Olivier Marie. After my Ph.D., I joined the University of Sydney in Australia as postdoctoral Research Associate, before joining the University of Melbourne in my current capacity. Before my Ph.D., I completed a M.Sc. degree in Statistics at Ensai in France, and a M.Sc. in Economics at Humboldt University in Germany.

title: Creating an academic website using RMarkdown
text:
These are the resources I used to make my own website. I tried different things (Wordpress, Squarespace, Jekyll…), and I find that the easiest way by far to create a static website is to use R and host your page via Github Pages. Github allows you to host your website for free, update it super quickly, and will never bug (unlike those sneaker ruby gem updates for your Jekyll page…) :-) Sure, you could make your page using Google Sites, but making your own page from scratch is much more fun!

Start from Emily Zabor’s super simple guide here. Run through the complete guide first, before tweaking the design.
Learn the basics of RMarkdown to create your own content:

RMarkdown basics here
More RMarkdown basics here
Making websites using RMarkdown here

Then tweak the design of your website by digging into more advanced topics using more complete guides:

This online book here
Yan Holtz’s RMarkdown tips here
Academic Icons (e.g. for your contact list) here

Note: for more control, you may want to learn a bit about HTML for organizing content and CSS for styling.

title: Academic Writing
text:
Writing is a core part of our work as academics. I am always surprised to hear my junior peers say that they will invest in their writing skills later on in their career, as if writing doesn’t matter for getting our papers published and actually surviving in academia. First of all, the quality of our prose DOES matter for getting our papers out (my co-author Jan Feld just published an experimental study on this!). Second, spending a bit of energy polishing our papers can be enjoyable, much like any craft that one hones with time. Here are some resources that I keep coming back to, especially when I need inspiration for writing:

the one and only Economical Writing by Deirdre McCloskey and Stephen Ziliak. This book is beautifully written, insightful and hilarious! I love their tip about writing down ideas on single pieces of paper or postits and playing with the order, and the tip about cutting every third word when polishing a text.

title: Research
text:
Child Health and Parental Responses to an Unconditional Cash Transfer at Birth, with John Lynch, Aurélie Meunier, Rhiannon Pilkington, and Stefanie Schurer.
(Conditionally Accepted at the Review of Economics and Statistics).



Abstract

We estimate the impact on child health of the unanticipated introduction of the Australian Baby Bonus, a $3,000 one-off unconditional cash transfer at birth. With population-level administrative data from South Australia and a regression discontinuity design, we find that eligible infants experienced fewer hospital presentations in the first year of life for preventable, acute, and severe problems. In auxiliary analyses using nationally-representative data, we find that the windfall cash allowed parents to increase expenditures on food and groceries, decreased financial stress and hardship, and improved physical and mental health. We calculate that 34% of the pay-out were recouped within the first year through lower health care costs.

Working Paper (April 2026) | IZA Discussion Paper (Sep 2021).
Slides NBER Summer Institute 2022 (July 2022).

Detecting Local Non-Compliance with Random Treatment Assignment in Quasi-Experiments, with an Application to Ability Peer Effects, with Nicolás Salamanca.
(Revise and Resubmit at the Journal of the European Economics Association).



Abstract

We develop a method to detect local non-compliance with a random treatment to recover valid quasi-experiments from existing data. Our approach combines simulation-based methods and latent class modelling in an intuitive way, can detect and characterize non-compliant risk sets, and is computationally undemanding. To illustrate its usefulness, we use it to estimate ability peer effects in Taiwan, where we have unusually rich data and a national mandate to randomly assign students to classrooms within schools, but with partial non-compliance. After recovering a valid quasi-experiment, we first estimate ability peer effects in line with other studies. We then document precisely estimated null effects on 18 potential mechanisms, many of which have been hypothesized but never tested. Our application shows how to use our method to expand the causal evidence base using existing datasets.

Latest Version (September 2024).
Older Version (“On the Mechanisms of Ability Peer Effects”, Dec 2020).
Media: The Conversation (Nov 2021) | ABC Radio Sydney Afternoons (15 Nov 2021).

Same-Sex Teacher Effects, with Jan Feld, Nicolás Salamanca and Ulf Zölitz.
(Revise and Resubmit at the Review of Economic Studies).



Abstract

The idea that students benefit from same-sex teachers has motivated many policies around the world aimed at reducing gender inequalities. However, we do not know the size or generalizability such same-sex teacher effects. We fill this gap by conducting a meta-analysis and our own study using data from 90 countries. Our meta-analysis summarizes the literature and highlights that studies are often underpowered and difficult to compare because they use different methods. Our multi-country study overcomes these shortcomings by providing many high-powered and comparable estimates. Those estimates are ideal for learning about the generalizability of an effect. Our results reveal an interesting pattern. In secondary education, same-sex teacher effects are positive for most countries and outcomes. In primary education, effects are more mixed. For example, we find negative same-sex teacher effects on test scores for about half the countries. Our paper showcases how we can use multi-country studies to learn about the generalizability of an effect.

University of Zurich Working Paper No. 438 (June 2023, Updated May 2024) | Website with interactive results.
Slides.

Integrating Minorities in the Classroom: The Role of Students, Parents and Teachers, with Krzysztof (Chris) Karbownik, Nicolás Salamanca and Yves Zenou.
(Under Review)


Abstract

We develop a multi-agent model of the education production function where investments of students, parents, and teachers are linked to the presence of minorities in the classroom. We then test the key implications of this model using rich survey data and a mandate to randomly assign students to classrooms. Consistent with our model, we show that exposure to minority peers decreases student effort, parental investments, and teacher engagement and it results in lower student test scores. Observables correlated with minority status explain less than a third of the reduced-form test score effect while over a third can be descriptively attributed to endogenous responses of the agents.

Newer version (June 2026).
CEPR Discussion Paper (April 2024).
Media: VoxEU Column. 
Other: Best Paper Award at the 2023 Australian Labour Econometrics Workshop.

Career Mentoring for Underrepresented Talent: Effects on Education, Employment and Innovation, with Juan David García González and Nicolás Salamanca.
(Registered Report Under Review)


Abstract

This Registered Report presents a causal evaluation of Semillero de Talentos, a low-cost mentoring program for Colombian applicants planning postgraduate studies abroad. The program targets high-achieving, underrepresented, and geographically mobile applicants whose later returns can be large. We exploit the program’s score-based selection in a fuzzy regression discontinuity design across 2,020 applicants and eight cohorts, and we study education, employment, innovation, and migration outcomes through LinkedIn and OpenAlex data. We can detect effects of 11.5 to 18.8 percentage points, commensurate with the precision of published null effects for comparable mentoring programs.




Time, Money, and Infant Health: The Consequences of Paid Parental Leave, with Serena Yu and Maryam Naghsh Nejad.



Abstract

We estimate the effects of introducing paid parental leave on infant health and health care use in a setting with universal access to health care. We exploit Australia’s 2011 reform through a difference-in-discontinuity design and administrative records covering all New South Wales births. We find a 1.3 and 1.2 percentage points decline in probability of any specialist visits and any prescription medications in the first year, and no effects on hospital and emergency presentations. The reduction in any medication use persist until age five and estimates are larger among young mothers who were least likely to have had employer leave. Survey data suggest that the reform eased financial strain and preserved employment, pointing to improved parental resources and time.


Pre-Analysis Plan.
NEW Working Paper (September 2026).

Reproduction Report on “Unpacking p-Hacking and Publication Bias”, with Nicolás Salamanca.



Abstract

Brodeur, Carrell, Figlio and Lusher (2023) present the first descriptive evidence on p-hacking and publication bias throughout the publication process in economics. Using data from the Journal of Human Resources, they show that 1) p-values in initial submissions present humping around the 10 and 5% significance thresholds, 2) the distribution of desk rejections shows more humping than that of papers sent for review, 3) favorable reviewer recommendations are positively related to statistical significance and 4) overall, the p-value distribution of initial and final versions of accepted drafts appear similar. We first conduct a mostly successful computational reproduction of those results. Next, we conduct a series of robustness replication exercises and show that, while the authors’ main results are robust to random removals of small amounts of data and to bandwidth choices, they are sensitive to removing papers that contribute many estimates, to some key modelling choices in density discontinuity tests, and to some conceptually equivalent variations of their tests. Last, we complement the authors’ results by providing statistical tests of their main hypotheses. Our results support the claims that 1) the distribution of p-values of desk-rejected papers displays greater bunching than that of papers sent for review, and 2) the distributions of p-values of initial submissions and final drafts are similar. Overall, our findings lend support to the authors’ main claims, suggesting that after excluding desk-rejected papers, the peer review process does not seem to affect p-hacking or publication bias.

Working Paper (May 2026).
Original Authors Response (June 2026).

title: Research
text:
Publications
The Sources of Researcher Variation in Economics, with Nick Huntington-Klein, Claus C. Pörtner and many others.
(Accepted at the Journal of Economic Literature).


Abstract

We use a rigorous three-stage many-analysts design to assess how different researcher decisions—specifically data cleaning, research design, and the interpretation of a policy question—affect the variation in estimated treatment effects. A total of 146 research teams each completed the same causal inference task three times each: first with few constraints, then using a shared research design, and finally with pre-cleaned data in addition to a specified design. We find that even when analyzing the same data, teams reach different conclusions. In the first stage, the interquartile range (IQR) of the reported policy effect was 3.1 percentage points, with substantial outliers. Surprisingly, the second stage, which restricted research design choices, exhibited slightly higher IQR (4.0 percentage points), largely attributable to imperfect adherence to the prescribed protocol. By contrast, the final stage, featuring standardized data cleaning, narrowed variation in estimated effects, achieving an IQR of 2.4 percentage points. Reported sample sizes also displayed significant convergence under more restrictive conditions, with the IQR dropping from 295,187 in the first stage to 29,144 in the second, and effectively zero by the third. Our findings underscore the critical importance of data cleaning in shaping applied microeconomic results and highlight avenues for future replication efforts.


SSRN Working Paper (February 2025).

Reproducibility and Robustness of Economics and Political Science Research (2026, Nature 652, 151-156), with Abel Brodeur, Derek Mikiola and many others.
(previously circulated as “Mass Reproducibility and Replicability: A New Hope”).



Abstract

This systematic and large-scale reproduction effort tests the reproducibility and robustness of economics and political science, contributing to a growing literature on research credibility and self-correction in science [1–4]. We reproduced original analyses and conducted robustness checks of 110 articles recently published in leading economics and political science journals, all of which have mandatory data and code sharing policies [17,18]. We found that over 85% of published claims were computationally reproducible. In robustness checks, our re-analyses led to 72% of statistically significant estimates to remain significant and in the same direction, and the median reproduced effect size is (nearly) the same as the originally published effect size (that is, 99% of the published effect size). Additionally, six independent research teams examined 12 pre-specified hypotheses about determinants of robustness. Research teams with more experience found lower levels of robustness, and robustness correlated with neither author characteristics nor data availability.


I4R Discussion Paper Series (April 2024).
Replication Data and Code.

Re-examining the relationship between patience, risk-taking, and human capital investment across countries (2024, Journal of Applied Econometrics, 1-9.), with Jan Feld, Nicolás Salamanca.



Abstract

Hanushek et al. (2022) show that students in countries in which people are more patient and less risk-taking perform better in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) test. In this paper, we probe the robustness of this study. Our narrow replication shows that the results are mostly robust to alternative model specifications. Our broad replication shows that the main results are robust to measuring student performance with data from The Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) and The Progress in International Reading Literacy Study (PIRLS) instead of PISA.


Replication Package

title: Research
text:
Selected Research in progress
Class Rank and Sibling Spillover Effects



Abstract

This paper studies how students’ relative rank affects their younger siblings’ academic performance. Using Dutch administrative data, I exploit within-school, across-cohort variation in student rank. Consistent with previous research, I find that higher-ranked students experience faster human capital accumulation. Yet, these rank effects generate negative spillovers on younger siblings: a one standard deviation increase in rank decreases younger sibling’s test scores by 2 percent of a standard deviation. These spillovers are stronger for same-sex siblings. I show that changes in parental investments and expectations drive part of these spillovers. In particular, I show that migrant parents increase investments in school quality and speaking Dutch at home. My findings highlight that the peer environment creates within-family human capital spillovers.


Draft JMP version (31 August 2022).

title: Research
text:
Permanent Working Papers
From Subsidies to Loans: The Effects of a National Student Finance Reform on the Choices of Secondary School Students, with Jan Kabátek.



Abstract

We analyse the effects of a national student finance reform in the Netherlands, which replaced universal subsidies for higher education students by low-interest loans. We show that this reform had a large impact on education choices of secondary school students, lowering their enrolments in college-preparing tracks and increasing the share of students specializing in STEM subjects. The reform also affected the living arrangements of new college entrants. Our findings highlight that secondary school students respond to the modes of higher education financing well ahead of their graduation, and that financial aid uncertainty alone can deter many from pursuing higher education.


IZA Discussion Paper (Aug 2021).

Two Decades of Welfare Reforms in Australia: How Did They Affect Single Mothers and Their Children?, with Stefanie Schurer and Angela Zhang.



Abstract

Worldwide, single mothers are profoundly time and income constrained, making them heavily reliant on government transfers. We examine how welfare reforms that introduced mutual obligations affected the economic position of single mothers and the development of their children over the past two decades in Australia. Using nationally representative longitudinal data, we show that disposable incomes of single-mother households were significantly reduced relative to partnered mothers since the 2005 Welfare-to-Work Act came into effect in July 2006, a downward trend that was aggravated by the Global Financial Crisis and the 2013 suspension of grandfathered single parenting payment rules. The reform diminished parenting and family payments for single mothers, who compensated income loss by increasing reliance on disability pension payments, work hours, and child-care expenditures. We then use nationally representative cohort data to estimate the impact of single motherhood on child skill development, following children who entered primary school when their mothers were affected by the Welfare-to-Work reform. We find unadjusted single-motherhood gaps of 0.2 SD in cognitive and 0.3 SD in non-cognitive skills. Non-cognitive skill gaps are only partially explained by differences in observable characteristics, while cognitive skill gaps are fully explained by observable characteristics. Differences in disposable household income between single and partnered mother households explain over 50% of the observed cognitive ability gaps in childhood and 25% in late adolescence. In the presence of positive spillover effects, we propose that welfare payments to vulnerable families may function as a social investment rather than a sunk cost.


IZA Discussion Paper (Sep 2021).

title: Why make a Pre-Analysis Plan
text:
I have always found that the most challenging part of working in academia is finding the right team. The right team can mean many things, but one of those things is having the same way of doing science. While it may seem obvious, it really isn’t. Like finding the right coach for you at sports, or finding the right partner in life, finding a good match is the difference between a successful long-lasting partnership and a painful experience with lasting harm to your self confidence. This is especially true in Economics where papers can take years until seeing the light of day in a peer-reviewed journal: being committed to a bad team for 5 years or more is 5 years or more of (unnecessary) headaches.
After several bad matches, I’ve become obsessed with finding ways to screen out bad matches as early as possible and avoid unnecessary struggle. It’s hard enough to do research as it is, that you don’t want to drag a bad team on top of that. You may want to screen teams on many things, but to me a central point is honesty. Honesty in your work, and honesty in how you communicate with and treat your partners.
As it turns out, honesty is a central aspect of good research practice in the emerging consensus from the science reform movement. There are as many ways of doing bad science–from p-hacking to hypothesis searching after knowing the results (HARKing)–, but we are now starting to see emerge a common framework for good research practice in quantitative fields, for example the FAIR data principles (see for example). These best practices essentially revolve around transparency, reproducibility and ethical conduct. There are many layers to each of these themes and people have different ways of applying those. To me, an important part of ethics includes the way we communicate with and treat each other in a team, especially those in positions of vulnerability–research assistants, Ph.D. students, postdocs, or anybody in a vulnerable position in the team. And sadly, academia is full of stories of horrible (male and female) supervisors and senior co-authors who treat their more junior peers like carpets.
One thing that I have found increasingly useful over the years is using pre-analysis plans as a screening device. What is a pre-analysis plan? A Pre-Analysis Plan is a document you write at the beginning of a project before producing any results in which you specify as many details as possible about the study. There are many guidelines and templates out there, here are a few good examples:

a template from the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in Social Sciences (BITSS)
a page with list of advice and checklist from J-Pal and an official guide here
a World Bank blog post from David McKenzie with a checklist

Even though most of the discussion around using Pre-Analysis Plans focuses on their use in experiments to reduce p-hacking and HARKing (see this excellent paper by Brodeur, Cook, Hartley and Heyes, 2024), my experience has been that they are especially useful for team work. Whether you are working on your own or with a team, writing down a Pre-Analysis Plan forces you to clarify the key elements of your project, the research question, the estimation strategy, the key outcomes, how you will measure them and handle multiple hypothesis testing, and the potential channels underlying the effects of interest. These are all things that you will inevitably have to write about later in drafting the paper, so it’s not a waste of time. On the contrary, this can form the basis of the eventual draft. More importantly, it saves you a ton of time when preparing your data because you open up your dataset knowing what is actually relevant for your project, and when estimating your effects of interest because you don’t get lost in specification searching which in any case is in the dangerous territory of p-hacking.
Beyond the clear advantage of bringing clarity, I see two lesser known advantages to Pre-Analysis Plans for team projects, whether experimental or not.
The first advantage is that they force the team to sit down and discuss all the details of how exactly they are going to conduct the research. In that sense, it reveals early disagreements that are bound to arise later in approaching data. For example, you have to specify a sequence such as not estimating any results until you have tested the assumptions underlying your research design, agreed on a specification and released the Pre-Analysis Plan.
The second advantage is that by asking the team to do this together, you immediately reveal who will be a problem on the team, either because of low engagement or because of questionable research practices. In other words, a Pre-Analysis Plan can be used as a screening device for team members, and can be a good way to signal that you care about your own research code of conduct.

title: Replicability and Reproducibility
text:
This is a topic that I find particularly important. I was lucky to have peers at Maastricht Uni with whom I could have great discussions about research practices, ethics and how to do our research the best we could – big shoutout to Henrik Zaunbrecher and to my amazing coauthors Jan Feld, Nicolás Salamanca and Ulf Zölitz for giving me so much food for thought. We talked a lot about the replication crisis and the file drawer problem (among many things). Here are some resources I’ve found over the years that have nourished my thoughts on this topic, and have helped me progress in my own practices.

This book Transparent and Reproducible Social Science Research by Garret Christensen, Jeremy Freese, and Edward Miguel. A fantastic introduction into the issues of the replicability problems, the incentive problems in modern science and practical advice to improve our research practices to move forward collectively. It’s also a relatively quick and easy read.

The Institute for Replication is a research lab led by Abel Brodeur and his team. They do amazing work to normalize replications, increase awareness around the need for replicating papers, and improving researchers’ incentives to replicate the work of others and make their own work more replicable. They have tons of teaching resources to transmit best practices to students, check out their website!

Data Colada is a great blog maintained by Profs. Uri Simonsohn, Leif Nelson and Joe Simmons. This blog is a gem: they keep the tone light but they always making you see things from a new perspective. They do some very serious data forensic work, write about best practices (e.g. I LOVE their post about the Groundhogday package for versioning in R), and propose new ways to detect p-hacking – among other topics.
People and institutions to follow who do very interesting work on meta-science: the BITSS (Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences), Simine Vazire and Fiona Fidler who co-direct the MetaMelb Research Group. I also find a lot of inspiration in the work and blog of Andrew Gelman and Rachael Meager.
A two-part podcast on Freakonomics Radio just came out about academic fraud. They invited some of the most influential researchers at the forefront of the discussions on meta-science and what we can do to improve research practices: Brian Nosek, Simine Vazire, Uri Simonsohn, Leif Nelson and Joe Simmons. Highly recommend both podcasts:

Part 1: EPISODE 572 Why Is There So Much Fraud in Academia?
Part 2: EPISODE 573 Can Academic Fraud Be Stopped?

title: The Double Failure of Bad Science
text:
I’ve been thinking a lot about the issues in this post over the past decade. Over the years, I ended up explaining to people around me why I think it’s important to participate in large-scale replications, to pre-register analyses, and so on. I am now writing this down as a way to wrestle with my thoughts, because writing is thinking. It helps me think through the deep reasons that drive me to do these activities.
In 2010, two prominent economists, Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff, published a paper called “Growth in a Time of Debt.” Looking at decades of data, they reported a striking pattern: countries with public debt above about 90 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) appeared to grow much slower than those below the threshold. Within months, the European Commission, US politicians, and Treasury officials across several countries were citing the 90 percent threshold to justify measures of austerity.
Three years later, a graduate student and two of his professors at the University of Massachusetts Amherst obtained the underlying spreadsheet. They found two problems: an Excel error that excluded several countries from the calculation, and results that turned out to be sensitive to how those countries’ growth experiences were weighted. Once the error was fixed, the dramatic threshold effect largely disappeared.
People usually tell this story as a scientific mistake. I think it is also about a second, subtler failure: policymakers rushing to implement fiscal austerity without discernment, at immense societal and political cost. Even if the original correlation had been correct, transplanting it across very different countries and historical eras as if it were a law of nature ignored the fundamental uncertainty of any research finding. This double failure durably eroded trust in both political institutions and science.
How much of the “evidence” behind “evidence-based” policy is this fragile? And how much do mistakes like the Reinhart and Rogoff study cost us? Both questions point to a shared duty. Researchers must produce the most reliable work they can. But those who consume that work, policymakers above all, have a responsibility to use it with discernment. A researcher cannot be held accountable for policymakers doing policy without investing the time to understand the evidence base.

title: The Double Failure of Bad Science
text:
Science is in crisis
The case of the Reinhart and Rogoff study is not an isolated incident. The recent decade has witnessed a crisis in science and public inquiry into the credibility of scientific findings.
Science has many issues, but we’ve seen it placarded all over the internet over the past decades. In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration found that fewer than half of the published psychology results it tried to reproduce held up. The following year, a team of economists led by Colin Camerer tried to replicate experimental economics papers from two of the most respected journals in the field. Only about 61 percent of articles replicated.
Beyond replication failure, there is also the issue of publication bias. Publication bias is the fact that the papers that get published are often a selection of the knowledge that is produced. For example, studies with large, striking findings are over-represented in the published literature, while studies that find no effect often don’t get published at all (the so-called “file drawer problem”). The issue with publication bias is that policymakers reading the literature only read a selected part of the evidence. I describe the crisis and my understanding of some of its causes in more detail in a separate post.
Why should we care that science is in crisis? Because bad science is waste in at least four ways.
First, misallocated funding. When the published record is incomplete or distorted, public research dollars chase questions that have already been studied (sometimes already answered negatively) because the relevant null results, the studies that found no effect, are sitting unread in someone else’s filing cabinet. Second, false leads. Like misallocated funding, bad science is a waste of other researchers’ time chasing false leads. Take for example the 2006 Lesné and Ashe paper in Nature, which placed a particular protein (Aβ*56) at the heart of Alzheimer’s and was retracted in 2024 after years of related work had been built on it. The cost is years of researcher-time and careers built on sand. This is especially costly to junior talent. Third, opportunity cost. The grant funding a flawed study is the grant that did not fund a sound one. Fourth, eroded public trust. The saddest and perhaps most telling example: Andrew Wakefield’s 1998 paper linking the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine to autism was retracted in 2010, but the damage to vaccine uptake and the subsequent measles resurgences are still with us.

title: The Double Failure of Bad Science
section: Scientific Reform: Fixing the production of science
text:
Scientific Reform: Fixing the production of science
Over the past two decades or so, a growing movement amongst scientists has pushed to improve the way we do science towards more transparency and more credibility. The broad agenda of the Open Science movement is to define best practices that allow the scientific community to catch mistakes throughout the scientific process, from openly sharing code and experimental protocols to systematically auditing published studies.
First, large-scale replications after publication. Many problems do not surface until someone tries to redo a paper that is already published. In economics, the Institute for Replication, launched in 2022, coordinates that work across economics journals, checking whether published findings hold up. The idea is to find mistakes, and to deter future data manipulation or fraud. In a study I took part in, published in Nature in 2026, we took 110 papers from top economics and political-science journals and tried to reproduce them: more than 85 percent could be reproduced from the data and code, but coding errors lurked in about a quarter, and the headline result held up under reasonable robustness checks (running the analysis again in other defensible ways) in only about 70 percent. Beyond catching errors, the work has changed incentives: for authors, knowing your paper may be audited makes you check it more carefully before submitting; for replicators, there are increasingly many avenues to publish their replication study.
Second, checking papers before they are published. Top journals are increasingly verifying before any paper goes to print that the results can be reproduced from the data and code. In economics, the American Economic Association now runs every accepted paper through a dedicated “Data Editor” team that re-runs the analysis. In psychology, the top journal Psychological Science has adopted the same model under the leadership of their editor Simine Vazire, my colleague at the University of Melbourne. This type of initiative catches the kind of error in Reinhart and Rogoff’s paper at the source.
Third, emptying the file drawer. Some fields are moving toward pre-registration and pre-analysis plans. In economics, for example, it is now standard for experimental work to release a document before collecting data (a pre-registration) explaining what the research team will measure and what would count as a meaningful finding. This makes it harder for null results to vanish into a drawer, because the original plan is on the record even if the study never makes it to a journal. Several journals also go further by publishing registered reports, articles accepted for publication solely on the basis of the research design, before any results are in. That way, the studies that find “nothing happened” get published too, and the evidence base is progressively less biased.
Fourth, catching honest mistakes. Artificial intelligence has enabled new tools designed to catch errors before papers go to print. Refine Technologies, an AI “peer reviewer” built by academics at Harvard and Northwestern and launched in 2025, scans manuscripts for inconsistencies and calculation errors in minutes. Tellingly, its founders open every pitch with Reinhart and Rogoff, exactly the kind of spreadsheet slip an automated check would have caught. We still do not know how far AI-based tools can push the credibility of scientific work, but many experts are hopeful that they can enhance the scientific process. See the development economist Edward Miguel’s recent panel on the question and a National Bureau of Economic Research session transcribed by Scott Cunningham.
This is by no means complete, there are many other ways and initiatives to improve science and scientific practices. My understanding is that all of these approaches share one thing in common: they all target the production of research to make new studies more reliable.
I think there is a remaining issue that I don’t see much debate about, which is how consumers of research interact with and interpret findings.

title: The Double Failure of Bad Science
section: Can we fix the consumption of science?
text:
Can we fix the consumption of science?
Consumers of science often have issues understanding scientific findings and deriving policy recommendations from them. The reaction to the latest PISA results shows how much policymakers want to learn from research. PISA is the OECD’s international test of 15-year-olds in reading, mathematics and science. The 2025 results, released in September 2026, recorded the lowest OECD-average scores so far in all three subjects. Since 2022, scores fell in reading and in mathematics in more than half of the countries with comparable data.
Governments reacted within days. In Australia, the Minister for Education, Jason Clare, declared that “the reading wars are over. We know what works to teach children to read,” and pointed to the reforms England rolled out almost twenty years ago. In Germany, the federal education minister, Karin Prien, called the results “dramatic” and said that, unlike at the time of the “PISA shock” of 2000, “today we know the answers.” In France, the education ministry called for a gain of 20 points by 2029, the equivalent of one year of learning. A few days before the release, the Conseil d’analyse économique, which advises the French Prime Minister, had published an action plan of “measures whose effectiveness has been demonstrated by research and international practice.” Slovenia announced a comprehensive reform of its education system, along with a new national institute to study the effects of education policies.
These reactions show that policymakers care deeply about adopting best practice in education policy. The point I make in this post is that we don’t really know how to digest the knowledge from the academic literature and derive best-practice education policies, and we don’t yet have the tools to do it. This is a point I recently made in a Parliamentary inquiry in Australia, and presented in a public hearing last week.
Even when a scientific finding is sound, we can waste it by transporting it badly, generalizing beyond its original context. In a famous study, the economist Eva Vivalt looked at the evidence base on development programs around the world and found that the settings where such programs had been studied were so diverse that taking one estimate and applying it elsewhere could be wrong by roughly 100 percent.
The evidence base behind much of what policymakers cite is thinner than it looks. Take peer effects in education, the idea that the classmates a young person studies alongside matter for what they learn. This topic has been at the heart of the debate on school choice and urban segregation. Yet almost everything we know about peer effects comes from a handful of universities that, for administrative reasons, randomly assigned roommates or classmates. A policymaker in Canberra deciding whether to give families more choice would be extrapolating from a tiny, highly selected sample that does not represent the diversity of Australian school-age children.
When that base is thin, the temptation is to take one famous number from one famous study and assume it applies everywhere else. Class size is the textbook example. Tennessee’s Project STAR experiment in the 1980s found that smaller classes produced large gains for elementary-school students. When California rolled out a similar policy statewide in the 1990s, the gains largely vanished, partly because the state could not hire enough qualified teachers fast enough, and partly because school districts implemented it differently. A minister wanting to know what class-size reduction would do in their schools cannot simply borrow Tennessee’s number.
Quebec’s universal childcare rollout in the late 1990s is another cautionary tale. The province moved an entire cohort of young children into heavily subsidized daycare, only to find a decade later that the program had not been able to maintain quality at scale, and that the cohort showed worse behavioral and mental-health outcomes than its peers in other provinces.
So what can we do about that? How can we fix how we consume scientific findings?
Well, we can start with conducting a meta-analysis on a given topic: we pool together every study on the given research question (say, what is the effect of having higher achieving peers in my classroom on my test scores?) and report the average. That is better than relying on one result from a famous study. But it returns an average across very different settings and often different implementations, when what the policymaker actually needs is evidence that speaks to a setting like theirs. In addition, meta-analysis cannot easily distinguish between differences caused by true heterogeneity (genuine differences between settings and populations) and differences caused by research styles. Some of the variation in research findings is irreducible: the way someone decided to code a variable among many, the way someone defined their main sample, whether they added controls in an analysis. In a recent study I took part in, 146 research teams were given the same dataset and asked the same policy question. Even working from identical numbers, they reached strikingly different conclusions. The spread between teams was large, and tightening the rules (telling teams exactly what statistical method to use) did not close it. What this study tells us is that behind every “the effect was X” there is a distribution of plausible estimates, not a single fact. We need to get comfortable with this uncertainty in the truth.
So when we take an estimate from one study and assume it will transport to a new setting, two things can go wrong at once. One, we ignore the variation that comes from researchers’ choices in producing the original estimate, and two, we ignore the variation that comes from genuine differences between settings and populations.

title: The Double Failure of Bad Science
section: New approaches for translating findings to policy
text:
New approaches for translating findings to policy
I think we need to go further and find new approaches for translating findings to policy. I see two ways to do that: 1) producing all the missing estimates from imperfect data, 2) combining settings and making them comparable.
First, to produce the missing estimates, we can recover data that has been produced but shelved because of imperfect experimentation. Many real-world policy experiments get shelved when the experimentation was not perfectly implemented, leaving expensive, unpublished data sitting in a drawer. Experiments that rely on random matching, such as the assignment of students to classrooms, patients to doctors or cases to judges, often fail in a few schools, hospitals or courts, because some institutions find ways to bypass the rule. With Nicolás Salamanca at the University of Melbourne, we have developed a statistical method, the Fishing Algorithm, to rescue these experiments, salvaging usable estimates from data that would otherwise be thrown away. We implemented this method to salvage a fantastic survey in Taiwan, one of a kind. In Taiwan, national law requires schools to assign students to classrooms at random. Schools do not fully comply with the mandate, and 102 of the 333 schools in the data assign students by ability in breach of it. Our tool fishes out those schools, and the remaining schools show that higher-scoring classmates raise student test scores. More usable experiments mean more evidence about more settings, directly addressing the thinness of data and evidence I described above.
Second, we can also combine settings and harmonize data to make them actually comparable. With my coauthors Ulf Zölitz (University of Zurich), Jan Feld (Victoria University of Wellington) and Nicolás Salamanca (University of Melbourne), we show this idea in our paper on same-sex-teacher effects. We take a single policy question, what happens when boys are taught by male teachers and girls by female teachers, and we estimate this effect across many settings using one consistent approach throughout. Once the methodology is held constant, the differences in our findings across settings reflect genuine differences across schools, classrooms or countries, not different research teams making different choices.
Our study on same-sex teacher effects in education illustrates why we cannot assume that effects from one place will transport to another. In this paper we study three million students in 90 countries, and we find two key results. The first result is that same-sex teacher effects on test scores in primary education are tiny, hover around zero and are positive in only half of the countries and negative in the other half. This means that trying to increase same-sex matching of students and teachers in primary school is a coin flip in terms of policymaking. It also means that foreign estimates may not transport well at all. Our findings indicate that massive hiring of male primary school teachers is not a reliable way to boost test scores for boys.
The second result is that same-sex teacher effects are, in contrast, small but universally positive in other dimensions: in primary school, student enjoyment of subjects and self-confidence, and in secondary school, effects on test scores, subject enjoyment, self-confidence and intentions to go into science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). Whether findings transport from one setting to another is a question we should study, because it’s really not obvious.
The bottom line is that in science, the norm is thin, lopsided, noisy evidence. In many areas of research, the answer to this problem is not to produce one more study. It is a disciplined way to pool what we already have, and to think carefully how results might apply in the next population or setting. We can be much less wasteful with the knowledge and data that we already have.
Responsibility is shared between producers of research and consumers of research. On the production side, researchers are raising the bar: data editors at journals, mass replication after publication, AI tools that catch coding mistakes, pre-registration and registered reports. But now we also need the consumer side to start using evidence with discernment, by learning to accept the uncertainty underlying every scientific finding.
The next spreadsheet error is already out there. Whether it sets policy will depend on both sides doing their job: the producer catching it, and the consumer refusing to build a country’s austerity on a single number that nobody bothered to check.

title: The crisis in science and some of its causes
text:
This post describes my understanding of the crisis in science and some of its causes. This post goes with The Double Failure of Bad Science, where I develop some thoughts on some solutions. I’ve written a bit about this topic a while back in an earlier post.
The recent decade has witnessed a crisis in science and public inquiry into the credibility of scientific findings. Scientific failures are embarrassing and a massive source of waste: waste of public money, waste of time, waste of careers and brains.
In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration found that fewer than half of the published psychology results it tried to reproduce held up. The following year, a team of economists led by Colin Camerer tried to replicate experimental economics papers from the American Economic Review and the Quarterly Journal of Economics, two of the most respected journals in the field. Only about 61 percent of articles replicated. To replicate a study is to run it again, with new participants or new data, and to check whether the same result comes out.
Since then, an emerging body of work has identified several culprits. The first culprit is studies that are too small to reliably detect what they claim to find, often leading to false claims (Ioannidis 2005, PLoS Medicine; Button et al. 2013 for neuroscience). With few participants, chance alone can produce a striking result. The smaller the study, the more likely it is that a striking result is a fluke.
The second culprit is protocols described too thinly for anyone else to faithfully repeat the experiment. A protocol is the full description of the way a study was run: the participants, the tasks they were given, and the way their answers were measured. When that description is incomplete, a second team cannot run the same study.
The third culprit is samples that are not representative of anyone, with most behavioral findings resting on “WEIRD” subjects, usually Western university students (Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan 2010). WEIRD stands for Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic. A result found among students at a few Western universities may not hold for the rest of the world.
Replication failure is one particular aspect of the scientific crisis. Another aspect is publication bias: because null effects are much harder to publish than striking results, the published scientific literature in many fields is biased towards attention-grabbing findings. A null effect means that the study found no sign that the treatment or the policy it tested made a difference. In those areas of research, studies with large, striking findings are over-represented, while studies that find null effects often don’t get published at all (the so-called “file drawer problem”). The name comes from the filing cabinet where those studies stay, unread. A policymaker reading the literature is reading a selected slice of the evidence.
Another aspect is scientific fraud. Albeit rare, scientific fraud never fails to make headlines and does contribute to the crisis of confidence (Diederik Stapel; the Gino and Ariely data-fabrication allegations). On the Gino and Ariely case, see the blog pieces by Data Colada (here and here) and the fantastic piece in the New Yorker. In a field where a fraudster has been uncovered, the rest of the field spends years cleaning up while public trust takes the hit. The cleanup can be just as long when no fraud is involved. See Susan Dominus’s New York Times Magazine account of what followed Amy Cuddy’s power-pose research (the claim that holding a confident posture for a couple of minutes changes a person’s hormones and behavior) after it failed to replicate.
Conflicts of interest are a related but distinct issue from fraud. A conflict of interest arises when the people who fund or run a study gain from one particular result. The long-running cultural belief that “breakfast is the most important meal of the day” began in large part as a marketing slogan from cereal manufacturers, including Kellogg’s, in the early twentieth century. It is hard to overstate how much industry-funded nutrition research and pharmaceutical-company studies have shaken the trust people have in medical and life sciences.
Importantly, however, genuine heterogeneity can also explain a “failed” replication. There are real differences across populations, or differences in institutions and incentives. A result that does not replicate in a new place may still be correct in the place where it was first found. I come back to this point in the main post.

title: The crisis in science and some of its causes
